pr_title: drivers: power_domain: Introduce a gpio monitor driver
pr_body:
Power rails of some peripherals are controlled externally.
This is a case in embedded controllers, where the power of
some I2C devices are managed by the main application
processor.

To ensure that zephyr drivers access the devices where is
powered on, introduce a "monitoring" power domain. It works
by registering interrupt handler with gpio a pin, so that
when power state changes, it will notify relevant drivers.

Fixes: #51349

Hey @marc-hb, this has the side effect of adding a new priority symbol and adopting it in the existing power domain drivers, I guess it's drivers/power_domain/power_domain_intel_adsp.c going from `CONFIG_KERNEL_INIT_PRIORITY_DEFAULT` to `CONFIG_POWER_DOMAIN_INIT_PRIORITY`. In https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/61961 the check was enabled and you hit a case where the priority was incoherent with the tree but was probably working because the respective init functions were not using any api in an uninitialized state, but in this case it's actually detecting that the order was correct before the patch and it is not after. Unfortunately the workaround is again to massage the priority numbers -- notice that the one reported in the error is not the actual priority but rather the sequence number in the init (unfortunately I had to redo the backend for that check for compiler compatibility and I can't get the actual priority number anymore).

If it can help clarify what's going on you can run `./scripts/build/check_init_priorities.py -v` before and after and see how it changed. Already have https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/64486 to address the script output being, admittedly, not very clear.

issue_context.title: Turn power domains on/off directly
comments:
> We're trying to model this using Zephyr's power domains. We would like to create a power domain for the external "power rail". If the power rail turns off, we want to notify the temperature sensor drivers, so the drivers don't attempt to communicate with an un-powered device.

Interesting use-case, what happens when the power rail goes down halfway through an I2C transaction? Is this even feasible to properly support?
Actually, in our case, the SCL and SDA lines are also pulled up to the Power Rail so the I2C transaction will just fail.

> > We're trying to model this using Zephyr's power domains. We would like to create a power domain for the external "power rail". If the power rail turns off, we want to notify the temperature sensor drivers, so the drivers don't attempt to communicate with an un-powered device.
> 
> Interesting use-case, what happens when the power rail goes down halfway through an I2C transaction? Is this even feasible to properly support?

An I2C bus error is expected in that case.  On the next I2C transaction the I2C controller driver attempts to recover the bus.

In our case, our temperature polling thread repeatedly generates I2C bus errors trying to read temperatures from the powered off devices.

review_comments: Why do you need to remove the callback if adding the callback failed?
Done

this can cause a problem, if a device under this domain calls `pm_device_runtime_put()`, the device will first be suspended then if this domain reference's count is 0, the subsystem will try to suspend this domain and return it as result of the `pm_device_runtime_pu()` operation.

It was already discussed here, but this domain is not really a power domain driver but a monitor ... it should probably just return 0 here since there is nothing a driver / subsys / application can do about it.
That's a good point and I can change it, but I'm not sure, I should. As a basis for PR, I've looked at a suggestion by @JordanYates in #51349. I think we should wait for his comment.
Ohh nevermind, you are not handling  `PM_DEVICE_ACTION_SUSPEND`.
Why  does this driver support PM at all? Given it is only monitoring a GPIO I can't see a use case for suspending or resuming it.

I want to support runtime PM. Every time `pm_device_runtime_get` is called, first power domain gets PM_DEVICE_ACTION_RESUME and then device can be resumed - only if ACTION_RESUME was successful on power domain.

The goal of a power domain is for dependent drivers to be configured appropriately for the power state they are physically in. If we consider a device on this power domain, where application code calls:
```
pm_device_runtime_get(dev);  <- Results in `PM_DEVICE_ACTION_TURN_ON` on the device
do things...
pm_device_runtime_put(dev); <- No callback run
k_sleep(K_SECONDS(3));
pm_device_runtime_get(dev); <- Results in `PM_DEVICE_ACTION_TURN_ON` on the device
do things...
pm_device_runtime_put(dev); <- No callback run
```
The device has had `PM_DEVICE_ACTION_TURN_ON` run on it twice, with no physical change in power state. This is not conducive to writing reliable drivers.
IMO this uncontrolled domain can only make sense if the actions are run only when the domain physically changes state.

Yes this seems more reasonable to me, succeeding to "Power up" the bus when it is already on, failing otherwise.
Minus the camel case, which should be `data->is_powered`.
Already updated files, now pm_action only check `is_powered` boolean and then returns proper value, `is_powered` is only changed during gpio callback.

Because this logic is triggered by external events, it has the potential to break the expected chain of events.
The expectation is a driver in ACTIVE will transition through SUSPENDED before going to OFF.
This driver will instead go straight from ACTIVE to OFF.

In monitoring power domain, there is no control over power rail, so going from ACTIVE to OFF is expected. When an interrupt is triggered, power domain notifies child nodes about the current state of rail. Monitoring power domain can't delay turning on/turning off power.

I understand the physical transitions, but implementing it in this way greatly complicates writing device drivers.
If `PM_DEVICE_ACTION_RESUME` allocates resources and `PM_DEVICE_ACTION_SUSPEND` releases them, that callback is now required to manually check on every call which state `PM_DEVICE_ACTION_TURN_OFF` is running from, in order to determine whether the resources have been freed yet or not. This is the model we explicitly moved away from in the transition to the `PM_DEVICE_ACTION_*` model.

I also understand that doing
```
pm_device_children_action_run(data->dev, PM_DEVICE_ACTION_SUSPEND, NULL);
pm_device_children_action_run(data->dev, PM_DEVICE_ACTION_TURN_OFF, NULL);
```
is not a great solution either, as `SUSPEND` is probably doing some communication with the device, which will obviously fail here.

The best solution I can think of here is an additional action `PM_DEVICE_ACTION_OFF_FROM_ACTIVE` which directly encodes this transition and makes it simple for drivers to handle. Thoughts @gmarull ?

I would choose to do two `PM_DEVICE_ACTION*` in sequence, it is easier to implement and does not require many changes to the existing code. Having a power bus that can change state at any time, it's expected that we don't care about shutting down devices correctly, so getting a bus error in that case is anticipated.

The other concern is that doing this in an asynchronous manner breaks the reference counting on device runtime PM. Standard power domains get around this by only running the actions when their own reference counts go to 0, which implies the child references are also 0.  I don't know if there is a reasonable solution to that.

Maybe custom visitor could solve this issue. By checking `pm->usage ` I could decide in what state the device should be. If `pm->usage > 0` than put a device in `RESUME`  state, otherwise put it in `SUSPEND`.
@JordanYates Friendly ping. Could you give an opinion on if a custom visitor is a good idea?

> Maybe custom visitor could solve this issue. By checking pm->usage  I could decide in what state the device should be. If pm->usage > 0 then put a device in RESUME state, otherwise put it in SUSPEND.

That doesn't handle the case of the reference count being `> 0` and the power domain going down. Manually setting the count to `0` will cause problems when running users try and call `pm_device_runtime_put`, and leaving it as it is will cause events to be run twice when the running users call `pm_device_runtime_put `.
@JordanYates Friendly ping
I suspect that is the best that is possible. Whether that is acceptable to others I don't know
I've uploaded changes as discussed in this thread. Can you take a look and give your opinion? If you believe there is somebody else that should give their feedback, feel free to add them.
